"SAD Lamps" - true full-spectrum light emitters meant for combatting seasonal affective disorder - are rather expensive medical devices. You can get much of the same effect putting daylight spectrum bulbs in some or all of your light fixtures, and they're much less expensive.

A quick explanation of "color temperature": When you heat something it glows. It'll glow red, then orange, yellow, and white. The color temperature is how hot you'd have to heat something for it to emit that light. Here is a chart of color temperatures; if it's a bright blue sky outside and you're in the shade, the color temperature you'll experience is 10,000 K. For our purposes, anything at or over 6,000 K will work as a "daylight spectrum bulb". If you look at a retail package of light bulbs one of the things it will tell you is the color temperature the bulb produces.

Here is an example of an inexpensive CF bulb. This has a color temperature of 2,700K, or "warm white", which matches the filament temperature of most cheap incandescent bulbs. They're often used decoratively, for dining and living rooms, where it can give a cozy, sleepy effect; but they're often used everywhere simply because they're not expensive.

This is an example of a daylight spectrum bulb. (It's labeled "full-spectrum" but I'm not sure if it actually is - more on that later.) These run roughly 50% more in price than lower temperature bulbs; they may also give the room an appearance you'd find unusual if you designed it around lower temperature lighting.

The difference between daylight spectrum and full spectrum is complicated... Fluorescent lights - and this includes LED bulbs, because they're actually also fluorescent-compound-based - utilize a mix of several phosphors which emit visible light when exposed to ultraviolet light. Their combined emissions do not provide a smooth spectrum compared with "black body radiation" - which is what the hot filament of a classic incandescent light bulb produces. A "daylight" bulb might leave out certain light frequencies which aren't present in a true full-spectrum emitter. Whether these frequencies have actual therapeutic value is uncertain.

Also important isn't only the color temperature of these lights, but how bright they are and long you spend exposed to it. If you're sitting in a dark room staring at the computer for much of the day, for instance, having lights around turned off or in rooms other than the one you're in aren't going to help you.
SAD Lamps are $$$. Try using daylight spectrum light bulbs in your fixtures instead
